clue.text: Cry, as time short for rejigging study of the universe

indicators.note: to rejig is to rearrange, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone protests that there is too little time for reorganising a cosmology course.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Cry' makes it look like a separate outburst, but it is simply the first three letters of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Astrochemistry studies the chemistry of stars and interstellar space, so it is a study of the universe.

clue.text: Volcanic region around Etna hot and saline

indicators.note: the letters are moved around, i.e. rearranged

parts.note: H = hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A description of the hot, salty landscape near Sicily's volcano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a position word placing something around Etna, but here it means 'rearranged'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Helena is a volcanic island in the South Atlantic, a British overseas territory.

clue.text: Summary concerning player in national team

parts.note: re = concerning, as in a memo heading
a cap is a player picked for the national side, who is 'capped'

explanation.surface: A report summing up an international player's match.
explanation.walkthrough: In British sport a player selected for their country receives a cap, and the player can be called a cap.
explanation.definitionFit: A recap is a short summary of what has happened.

clue.text: Ratified two companies welcoming new editor

parts.note: CO = company, the first of the two
a firm is the second company

explanation.surface: Two businesses approve a deal while taking on a fresh editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two companies' needs two different words for a business, one abbreviated and one in full, with the N welcomed between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To confirm an agreement is to ratify it.

clue.text: Oriental festival ending in altercation

indicators.note: take the ending, the last letter, of 'altercation'

explanation.surface: An Asian festival that finishes in a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ending in' reads as though the festival ended badly; it just points to the N at the end of altercation.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'Oriental' describes things from Asia, the lands to the east.

clue.text: Basic accommodation's one good toilet?

parts.note: loo is British slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: A review of a basic lodging praising its one decent toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in 'accommodation's' is 'has', joining definition to wordplay; the question mark flags an igloo as a playful example of basic accommodation.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is a simple shelter made of snow blocks, about as basic as accommodation gets.

clue.text: Harry tethering spanner, perhaps?

indicators.note: to harry is to harass or disturb, so the letters are disturbed

explanation.surface: Someone called Harry ties up a spanner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' poses as a name at the start of the sentence; it is the verb 'to harry'. The question mark says a spanner is only one kind of tightener.
explanation.definitionFit: A spanner tightens nuts, so it is an example of a tightener.

clue.text: Coyest nurses agreed

definitions.note: 'Agreed!' as an interjection, the same as 'Yes!'

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold closely, so the word holds the answer

explanation.surface: The shyest nurses consented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' looks like a noun for hospital staff but is the verb, meaning 'holds'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'Agreed!' is saying 'Yes!'.

clue.text: Conductor unknown in Cuba

parts.note: algebra's unknowns are x, y and z
C is Cuba's international vehicle registration code

explanation.surface: An orchestra conductor whose whereabouts in Cuba are a mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests a musician, but it is a metal that conducts electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: Zinc is a metal and a good conductor of electricity.

clue.text: No substance protects unaccompanied medic

parts.note: the gist is the substance of something

explanation.surface: A doctor working alone is left without cover, a remark with no substance behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No substance' reads as a single phrase, but it is two pieces that open to hold 'unaccompanied'. A nosologist is a rare word for a medical classifier of diseases.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosologist is a medical specialist who classifies diseases.

clue.text: I ate carp, unfortunately with bad consequences

indicators.note: the letters have come out badly, i.e. in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A diner regrets eating a carp, which did not agree with them.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs straight into the definition: eating the carp did come at a price.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done 'at a price' is achieved only with unpleasant consequences.

clue.text: Do not change income, essentially, for backing groups

parts.note: stet is the proofreader's mark meaning 'leave as it was'
the middle two letters of inCOme

explanation.surface: Advice to keep earnings the same in order to fund backing singers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing groups' looks like a single phrase for support bands, but 'backing' is the reversal and 'groups' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Octets are groups of eight, especially of musicians.

clue.text: Right-winger, originally Trotskyist, that Blair, perhaps, welcomes

parts.note: Cherie Blair, wife of the former Labour prime minister Tony Blair

indicators.note: the original, first, letter of Trotskyist

parts.note: its first letter, placed inside CHERIE

explanation.surface: Tony Blair's embrace of a former far-left figure turned right-winger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blair, perhaps' invites Tony, but the Blair needed is his wife Cherie. A Thatcherite supports the policies of Margaret Thatcher, the Conservative prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: A Thatcherite follows Margaret Thatcher's free-market Conservative politics, so is right-wing.

clue.text: Reason for illness, oddly, lies in Soho obsession

indicators.note: take the odd-numbered letters of the words that follow

parts.note: the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th letters: L, E, I, S, H

explanation.surface: An illness blamed on untruths told amid a fixation with Soho, London's nightlife district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' seems to comment on the illness, but it acts on the three words after it, running across the space between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Leishmania is the parasite that causes leishmaniasis, so it is the cause of an illness.

clue.text: Stokes tricking Beefy

parts.note: S is an abbreviation for stokes, a unit of viscosity
to trap someone is to trick them

explanation.surface: England all-rounder Ben Stokes outwitting Ian Botham, the cricketer nicknamed Beefy.
explanation.walkthrough: Both capitals are camouflage: Stokes and Beefy are famous English cricketers, but here one is a unit and the other just means 'burly'.
explanation.definitionFit: A strapping person is big and strong, which is what beefy means.

clue.text: Husband to leave pet with mother in city

parts.note: a dam is an animal's mother

explanation.surface: A husband walks out, leaving the family pet with his mother in town.
explanation.walkthrough: The domestic scene hides the mechanics: the husband does not leave the pet, he leaves it, the H dropping out of HAMSTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Dutch capital is one of many cities.

clue.text: Orderly content to chaperone a therapist

indicators.note: the answer is the content of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A hospital orderly who is happy to accompany a therapist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orderly content' reads as a contented hospital porter; 'content' is the noun, what the phrase contains.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat and orderly both mean tidy and well arranged.

clue.text: Listen to them fart endlessly

indicators.note: both words lose their ends, first and last letters

explanation.surface: A crude invitation to listen to people breaking wind non-stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' seems to describe how long they go on, but it strips the outer letters from each word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as in a judge who agrees to hear, that is listen to, a case.

clue.text: Shocked, calls business receiving millions

parts.note: to dub is to call or name
truck means dealings, as in 'have no truck with'

explanation.surface: Someone stunned to hear of a company raking in millions.
explanation.walkthrough: Truck in the old sense of trade or dealings survives in the phrase 'have no truck with'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: struck dumb, too shocked to speak.

clue.text: Great footballer, I see, is saviour

explanation.surface: A fan declares a great footballer their saviour.
explanation.walkthrough: Fans really do hail star players as saviours, so the surface and the answer share a scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the Hebrew for 'anointed one', the deliverer awaited in Judaism and identified with Christ in Christianity.

clue.text: Boost sheep chased by young dog

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep
a pup is a young dog

explanation.surface: A sheep being chased by a puppy speeds up.
explanation.walkthrough: The farmyard chase sets the order: the sheep in front, the pup behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the image of climbing a ramp: to increase output or effort step by step.

clue.text: Writer skirts around tree

explanation.surface: An author walks the edge of a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like part of the instruction but it is the thing contained, CA; 'skirts' is the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: The pecan is a North American hickory tree.

clue.text: What Santa did to get around greatly impressed, it's said

definitions.text: What Santa did to get around

indicators.note: signals a word that sounds like the answer

parts.note: 'slayed' is slang for impressed hugely, as in 'she slayed it'

explanation.surface: A joke about how Father Christmas travels and how his performance wowed the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a playful description rather than a synonym: Santa travels by sleigh.
explanation.definitionFit: Santa goes about by sleigh, so he sleighed; the verb is coined for the joke.

clue.text: Perhaps Zack Polanski about to probe data

parts.note: gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, examines some figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks Polanski as one example of a Green, a member of the Green Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Zack Polanski leads the Green Party of England and Wales, so he is a Green.

clue.text: British Rail director taking small measure is good idea

parts.note: used as itself, split around INCH
an inch is a small unit of length

explanation.surface: A British Rail boss's cost-cutting plan hailed as inspired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'British Rail' reads as one name, the old national railway, but it splits into B and RAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A brainchild is someone's original idea or invention.

clue.text: Staff cross, but half-heartedly

parts.note: a rood is a cross, especially a crucifix in a church
one O of the middle OO removed

explanation.surface: Employees annoyed, though not very strongly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' and 'cross' read as angry workers; staff is a stick and cross is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a staff is a long stick, as a shepherd or pilgrim carries.

clue.text: Give out terms of reference with no introduction

parts.note: a remit is a set of terms of reference
REMIT minus its first letter R

explanation.surface: Issuing a brief to someone without introducing it first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terms of reference' is a single phrase standing for REMIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To emit is to give out, as of light, heat or sound.

clue.text: Selfish spoilsport to prepare trap — those people infuriate

parts.note: to do vegetables is to prepare them
a gin is a snare or trap

explanation.surface: A selfish killjoy sets a trap, and it drives people mad.
explanation.walkthrough: The word breaks of the answer ignore the pieces, so 'dog' and 'manger' never appear whole in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog in the manger, from Aesop, spitefully withholds from others what they cannot use themselves.
